newsitem.title: IRAQ: UN says jets, US missiles at Iraq violate zone.
newsitem.headline: UN says jets, US missiles at Iraq violate zone.

text.p: The United Nations said recent U.S. missile attacks on Iraq and overflights on Wednesday by unidentified warplanes had violated an Iraq-Kuwait demilitarised zone set up after the Gulf War.

Major-General Gian Santillo, Force Commander of the U.N. Iraq-Kuwait Observer Mission (UNIKOM), told Reuters two warplanes seen on Wednesday circling over the border had broken the terms of the 15 km (10 mile)-wide, U.N.-mandated zone.

He added in an interview UNIKOM observers had seen some of the 44 U.S. cruise missiles fired at targets in southern Iraq on September 3 and 4 fly over the zone. UNIOKOM sources said eight of the Tomahawks were sighted.
"It (missile strikes) was a violation," Santillo, an Italian, said, adding UNIKOM had reported both the overflights and the missiles to U.N. headquarters in New York.
Western diplomats said they did not expect a diplomatic incident over the UNIKOM report, saying it was a "theoretical" matter than had not been an issue at U.N. headquarters.
For six years Baghdad has faced international isolation and tough economic sanctions imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
"Overflying the DMZ (demilitarised zone) is a violation...I must say that now there are rare occasions but in the past maybe there were more," said Santillo, 10 months into his assignment.
"It does constitute a violation...any military hardware in the DMZ (demilitarised zone) from any parties constitutes a violation...No one is allowed to enter our DMZ".

UNIKOM tries to ensure no military activity occurs in the zone straddling the 207 km (130 mile)-long land border up to where the Iraq-Kuwait-Saudi Arabia border meets and a 40 km (25 mile)-sea border.

They must ensure no military force is present in the zone, which extends 10 km (six miles) into Iraq and five km (three miles) into Kuwait. Only police from Kuwait and Iraq are allowed into the DMZ with sidearms.
Santillo said he believed his force of some 200 unarmed observers and a 770-man Bangladeshi mechanised battalion was not in danger during the missile attacks.
"Inside the DMZ there are no military objectives," he said, adding the strikes were probably further away as observers did not see any smoke or flames.
He declined to say if the United Nations, like some countries, was informed in advance by Washington of the attack.

South of the DMZ, Washington will soon deploy some 3,500 ground troops. On Tuesday a battery of U.S. anti-missile Patriots was installed by Kuwait City in case the current standoff with Baghdad escalates.

Santillo said it was impossible to verify the nationality of the jets seen on Wednesday. The two aircraft, which broke the sound barrier over the DMZ, were apparently part of the force enforcing a Western-imposed no-fly zone in southern Iraq. The zone is not included in U.N. 1990-91 Gulf crisis-related resolutions.

The low-flying jets entered Kuwait at least twice on Wednesday from the north and turned back towards Iraq. Military sources said UNIKOM relies on the naked eye to record such violations, which makes it difficult to detect U.S., French and British patrol aircraft at high altitudes.
